messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tax Inspector
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Tired: Feeling very tired or exhausted, Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable, Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Minh is a 51-year-old Vietnamese American man who works as a tax inspector for a regional government office. He was referred for psychological assessment following a disclosure to his primary care physician of ongoing sleep difficulties, hypervigilance, and intrusive memories connected to a period of sustained physical abuse perpetrated by his former domestic partner, which ended approximately three years ago. His current PCL-5 score of 39 places him in the clinically significant range, and he presents as guarded but cooperative, speaking carefully and with long pauses.

The abuse unfolded over several years in what Minh had understood to be a committed relationship. His former partner's violence was characteristically unpredictable — erupting without warning from ordinary evenings, often when Minh had returned home exhausted after long hours at work. He recalls one night in particular: he had come home fatigued after a difficult audit cycle, sat down at the kitchen table, and within minutes found himself shielding his face from blows. There was no argument, no escalation he could trace. The randomness of it was, in some ways, the most damaging feature — because it meant that any moment of tiredness or discomfort, any situation he could not read in advance, became indistinguishable from the conditions that had preceded violence. He had learned, at a physiological level, that exhaustion and unpredictability were not merely unpleasant states but signals of imminent danger.

In the years since leaving, Minh has found that these same states reliably pull him back. When he feels the particular heaviness of fatigue at the end of a working day — sitting at his desk reviewing returns, or driving home through familiar streets — his body responds as though the threat is present: his heart rate climbs, he finds himself scanning doorways, pressing his back to whatever solid surface is nearest so that the room remains visible ahead of him. He frequently checks over his shoulder when walking between office floors, certain in those moments that someone is close behind him. He knows, intellectually, that nothing is wrong; yet the alarm is total and convincing. These episodes of perceived threat, in turn, are themselves triggering — the physiological arousal and the posture of vigilance recreate something close enough to the original conditions of danger that fragments of memory begin to surface unbidden: a hand raised, the sound of a chair scraping, the particular quality of silence that preceded the worst nights. These fragments arrive suddenly and without coherence, then vanish before he can examine them, leaving him disoriented. There are portions of those years he cannot access at all, no matter how deliberately he tries, which troubles him in its own way.

When the memories do force themselves through, they carry with them a weight of interpretation that has, over time, hardened into conviction. Minh has come to believe that he was fundamentally betrayed — not merely hurt, but deceived at the level of identity, by someone he had trusted completely. From this, a broader and more damaging conclusion has followed: that he is not a person to whom good things happen, that the future holds nothing he can reasonably hope for. He describes himself, haltingly, as feeling like an object in his own life — acted upon, without agency or worth. These appraisals do not remain static; they actively shape his daily experience. Because he believes himself to be without a meaningful future and essentially without personhood, ordinary discomforts and uncertainties feel freighted with confirmation — any unpredictable moment at work, any colleague whose mood he cannot read, registers immediately as potential threat, returning him to the vigilant scanning and the intrusive fragments that characterise his worst days. The cycle is self-sustaining in a way he has begun to recognise but cannot interrupt alone.

Minh has been married for six years to a woman he describes as patient and kind, though he acknowledges that his hypervigilance and emotional withdrawal have placed significant strain on their relationship. His wife recently told him she no longer recognises him at home. It was this — more than the sleeplessness, more than the checking and the scanning — that finally brought him to seek help. What he fears most is that nothing can be different. What he hopes, cautiously, is that he might be wrong about that.
